{{Short description|Mathematical theorem in real analysis}}
[[Image:Drini nonuniformconvergence SVG.svg|thumb|350px|right|Counterexample to a strengthening of the uniform limit theorem, in which pointwise convergence, rather than uniform convergence, is assumed. The continuous green functions <math>\scriptstyle \scriptstyle\sin^n(x)</math> converge to the non-continuous red function.  This can happen only if convergence is not uniform.]]

In [[mathematics]], the '''uniform limit theorem''' states that the [[uniform convergence|uniform limit]] of any sequence of [[continuous function]]s is continuous.

==Statement==
More precisely, let ''X'' be a [[topological space]], let ''Y'' be a [[metric space]], and let &fnof;<sub>''n''</sub>&nbsp;:&nbsp;''X''&nbsp;&rarr;&nbsp;''Y'' be a sequence of functions converging uniformly to a function &fnof;&nbsp;:&nbsp;''X''&nbsp;&rarr;&nbsp;''Y''.  According to the uniform limit theorem, if each of the functions &fnof;<sub>''n''</sub> is continuous, then the limit &fnof; must be continuous as well.

This theorem does not hold if uniform convergence is replaced by [[pointwise convergence]].  For example, let &fnof;<sub>''n''</sub>&nbsp;:&nbsp;[0,&nbsp;1]&nbsp;&rarr;&nbsp;'''R''' be the sequence of functions &fnof;<sub>''n''</sub>(''x'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;''x<sup>n</sup>''.  Then each function &fnof;<sub>''n''</sub> is continuous, but the sequence converges pointwise to the discontinuous function &fnof; that is zero on [0,&nbsp;1) but has &fnof;(1)&nbsp;=&nbsp;1.  Another example is shown in the adjacent image.

In terms of [[function space]]s, the uniform limit theorem says that the space ''C''(''X'',&nbsp;''Y'') of all continuous functions from a topological space ''X'' to a metric space ''Y'' is a [[closed set|closed subset]] of ''Y<sup>X</sup>'' under the [[uniform metric]].  In the case where ''Y'' is [[Complete metric space|complete]], it follows that ''C''(''X'',&nbsp;''Y'') is itself a complete metric space.  In particular, if ''Y'' is a [[Banach space]], then ''C''(''X'',&nbsp;''Y'') is itself a Banach space under the [[uniform norm]].

The uniform limit theorem also holds if continuity is replaced by [[uniform continuity]].  That is, if ''X'' and ''Y'' are metric spaces and &fnof;<sub>''n''</sub>&nbsp;:&nbsp;''X''&nbsp;&rarr;&nbsp;''Y'' is a sequence of uniformly continuous functions converging uniformly to a function &fnof;, then &fnof; must be uniformly continuous.

Both continuity and uniform continuity cases can be formulated in a more general context where <math>Y</math> (rather than being a metric space) is a [[uniform space]], in which the notions of [[Uniform convergence#Generalizations|uniform convergence]] and [[Uniform continuity#Generalization to uniform spaces|uniform continuity]] can still be defined. However, in this setting, the use of [[Net (mathematics)|nets]] or [[Filters in topology|filters]] is preferred over sequences for greater generality.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bourbaki |first=Nicolas |title=General Topology 2 |publisher=Hermann |year=1966 |location=Paris, Boulevard Saint-Germain |pages=280-283 |language=en}}</ref>

==Proof==
In order to prove the [[Continuous function|continuity]] of ''f'', we have to show that for every ''ε'' > 0, there exists a [[neighbourhood (mathematics)|neighbourhood]] ''U'' of any point ''x'' of ''X'' such that:

:<math>d_Y(f(x),f(y)) < \varepsilon, \qquad\forall y \in U</math>

Consider an arbitrary ''ε'' > 0. Since the sequence of functions ''(f<sub>n</sub>)'' converges uniformly to ''f'' by hypothesis, there exists a natural number ''N'' such that:

:<math>d_Y(f_N(t),f(t)) < \frac{\varepsilon}{3}, \qquad\forall t \in X</math>

Moreover, since ''f<sub>N</sub>'' is continuous on ''X'' by hypothesis, for every ''x'' there exists a neighbourhood ''U'' such that:

:<math>d_Y(f_N(x),f_N(y)) < \frac{\varepsilon}{3}, \qquad\forall y \in U</math>

In the final step, we apply the [[triangle inequality]] in the following way:

:<math>\begin{align}
  d_Y(f(x),f(y)) & \leq d_Y(f(x),f_N(x)) + d_Y(f_N(x),f_N(y)) + d_Y(f_N(y),f(y)) \\
                     & < \frac{\varepsilon}{3} + \frac{\varepsilon}{3} + \frac{\varepsilon}{3} = \varepsilon, \qquad \forall y \in U
\end{align}</math>


Hence, we have shown that the first inequality in the proof holds, so by definition ''f'' is continuous everywhere on ''X''.

==Uniform limit theorem in complex analysis==
There are also variants of the uniform limit theorem that are used in complex analysis, albeit with modified assumptions. 

'''Theorem.<ref>Theorems 5.2 and 5.3, pp.53-54 in E. M. Stein and R.Shakarchi's Complex Analysis.</ref>'''
Let <math>\Omega</math> be an open and connected subset of the [[complex number]]s. Suppose that <math>(f_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}</math> is a sequence of holomorphic functions <math>f_n:\Omega\to \mathbb{C}</math> that converges uniformly to a function <math>f:\Omega \to \mathbb{C}</math> on every compact subset of <math>\Omega</math>. Then <math>f</math> is holomorphic in <math>\Omega</math>, and moreover, the sequence of derivatives <math>(f'_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}</math> converges uniformly to <math>f'</math> on every compact subset of <math>\Omega</math>.

'''Theorem.<ref>Section 6.44, pp.200-201 in E. C. Titchmarsh's The Theory of Functions. Titchmarsh uses the terms 'simple' and 'schlicht' (function) in place of 'univalent'.</ref>'''
Let <math>\Omega</math> be an open and connected subset of the complex numbers. Suppose that <math>(f_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}</math> is a sequence of univalent<ref>Univalent means holomorphic and injective.</ref> functions <math>f_n:\Omega\to \mathbb{C}</math> that converges uniformly to a function <math>f:\Omega \to \mathbb{C}</math>. Then <math>f</math> is holomorphic, and moreover, <math>f</math> is either univalent or constant in <math>\Omega</math>.
